common_name: Amethyst Improved Basil (Genovese-Type Dark Purple Basil)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all danger of frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this improved selection holds classic sweet Genovese flavor and resists bolting better than earlier purple basil strains.

directions: Amethyst Improved is a refined selection of purple Genovese-type basil, with thick, turned-down, nearly black-purple leaves and pink flowers. Unlike many purple basils that lean toward clove-heavy or bolt-prone flavor profiles, this strain keeps the sweet, mild, true Italian basil taste of green Genovese types while holding its foliage quality and resisting premature flowering longer than the original Amethyst release. Pinch flower buds regularly and harvest stem tips often to keep plants bushy and productive through the season. Its deep color makes it a popular garnish and infusion basil as well as a culinary leaf basil.

common_name: Dartington Curry Plant (Compact Dark Silver Curry Plant)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after last frost in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this compact English selection does not come reliably true from seed.

directions: Dartington is a dwarf, tightly mounding form of curry plant selected for darker, more silvery-grey needle-like foliage than the straight species, with the same strong curry-like aroma released when the leaves are brushed or crushed. Its compact habit suits rock gardens, gravel plantings, and container culture better than the larger, more sprawling wild type. Grow in poor to average, very free-draining soil in full sun, and keep it dry over winter since soggy roots in cold weather are the most common cause of loss. Trim lightly after the small mustard-yellow flower clusters fade in summer to maintain a dense shape and prevent the center from going woody and bare.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after last frost in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; propagate by cuttings since this dwarf selection is not reliably seed-true.

directions: Korma is a particularly dwarf curry plant cultivar, forming a dense, low mound of fine, silvery, curry-scented foliage that stays noticeably smaller than both the species and other compact selections. It suits edging, small rock gardens, and pots where a full-size curry plant would quickly outgrow the space. Site it in poor, gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid winter wet, which is the main threat to its survival in marginal zones. Shear lightly in spring to remove any winter dieback and keep the mound tight and tidy.
sources: Specialist UK herb nurseries (e.g. Jekka's Herb Farm plant lists)

planting.note: Start indoors about 6-8 weeks before last frost, lightly scarifying and surface-sowing seed since light aids germination; transplant out after frost danger passes into well-drained, average soil in full sun.

directions: Schizonepeta tenuifolia, known in Traditional Chinese Medicine as jing jie, is an upright annual mint-family herb with finely dissected, aromatic leaves and slender spikes of small purple flowers resembling a lavender-flowered catnip. It is grown as a warming, exterior-releasing medicinal herb, typically dried for tea or decoction rather than used fresh in cooking. Give it full sun and average, well-drained soil; it tolerates poor fertility but grows lankier and may need light staking in rich, moist conditions. Harvest the flowering tops and upper leafy stems once blooms open, then dry quickly out of direct sun for later use.
sources: Mountain Gardens Herbs — Notes on Chinese Materia Medica for American Gardens

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings after last frost in moist, fertile soil; like other named mint selections it will not come true from seed, so propagate vegetatively.

directions: Candy Lime Mint, one of the named scented-mint selections popularized by herb breeder Jim Westerfield, produces fresh leaves with a distinctly sweet, candy-like lime aroma that nurseries note actually intensifies overnight after cutting. Use the leaves fresh in drinks, desserts, and fruit salads where a bright citrus-mint note is wanted without the sharper bite of true peppermint. Grow in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, and confine the spreading rhizomes with a buried edging strip or container since it spreads as aggressively as other mints. Cut plants back hard after flowering to encourage a flush of fresh, more strongly scented new growth.
